sourceTitle: Why Did That Message Sound Rude?
scoreRule: 1 point per correct MC item; 10 points maximum; local provisional grade only
description: Ten independent interpretation, argument and critical-transfer questions, pending teacher review.

questions.q: What makes a brief written reply especially open to misinterpretation?
choices: The reader lacks the voice and surroundings that would clarify its intent.
Written messages never contain meaningful information.
The sender can always see the reader's facial expression.
Punctuation has exactly the same effect in all groups.
questions.explanation: The opening explains that messaging strips away voice, expression and quick correction.

questions.q: Why may identical words convey different impressions at different times?
choices: The text automatically changes its meaning after three hours.
Readers can mistake a delay for a sign of the sender's attitude.
Every late reply has deliberately been postponed.
Short replies cannot be understood outside office hours.
questions.explanation: The article shows how time and context affect interpretation of the same message.

questions.q: What assumption led Dana to abandon the photo-book idea?
choices: Marek had voted for a completely different gift.
The teacher had already received the book.
She treated Marek's short agreement as hidden disapproval.
The group could no longer afford a present.
questions.explanation: Dana read a positive but ambiguous reply negatively without checking what it meant.

questions.q: Why does the writer specify that the group-chat example is invented?
choices: To suggest that such misunderstandings never happen.
To show that all group messages are fictional.
To avoid explaining why the gift was delayed.
To illustrate a common mechanism without claiming to report an actual case.
questions.explanation: The example is framed as a realistic invented scenario supporting the argument.

questions.q: Why would requiring formal messages everywhere be a poor solution?
choices: It would make the senders unable to correct spelling.
It could create new problems by ignoring the group's normal style.
It would eliminate every possible misunderstanding.
It is technically impossible to type long messages.
questions.explanation: The article rejects an excessively formal universal rule and advocates context-sensitive clarity.

questions.q: What principle connects the advice to ask questions and to use calls?
choices: Always choose the fastest communication platform.
Make difficult conversations visible to everyone.
Avoid disagreement by leaving messages unanswered.
Choose clarification over guessing what another person intended.
questions.explanation: Both suggestions help restore missing context instead of treating assumptions as facts.

questions.q: A teammate replies 'fine' to an important decision. What is the strongest next step?
choices: Ask whether they approve before making changes to the plan.
Cancel the idea without consulting them.
Assume their reply must be sarcastic.
Stop answering until they apologize.
questions.explanation: The Dana and Marek episode demonstrates the cost of assuming a meaning.

questions.q: A grandparent ends every text with a full stop. How should a younger relative respond?
choices: Treat every sentence as an angry warning.
Demand that the grandparent never use punctuation.
Consider that it may reflect ordinary punctuation rather than hostility.
Wait several days before replying in protest.
questions.explanation: Different generations may interpret the same form of punctuation differently.

questions.q: A class group keeps misunderstanding what a thumbs-up means. What could help?
choices: Ban every symbol without discussing it.
Agree on what the symbol means within that group.
Use the symbol more often without clarification.
Ask one person to guess its meaning for others.
questions.explanation: The article describes shared signals as a way of removing ambiguity.

questions.q: Two friends are discussing a painful disagreement by text. Which change fits the conclusion?
choices: Reply with shorter messages and no explanation.
Forward the conversation to a larger group.
Use a single 'OK.' to end the topic.
Move to a call or an in-person conversation when possible.
questions.explanation: A call can restore tone and speed up clarification when the subject is emotional.
